title: Circuits, Adders, and Subtractors
summary: Boolean functions become combinational circuits: from gate symbols and canonical DNF to half and full adders and multi-bit adders. Ripple-carry and conditional-sum adders show the trade-off between gate cost and circuit depth. Two's complement enables subtraction with an adder; signed overflow is detected from the carries at the sign bit.
keyFacts: A combinational circuit is a directed acyclic graph with no memory; its outputs depend on the current inputs.
In DIN/IEC symbols, ≥1 denotes OR; a small circle indicates negation.
The canonical DNF forms a minterm for each truth-table row with output 1 and combines the minterms with OR.
Cost C counts gates; depth D counts the gates on the longest input-to-output path.
A half adder adds two bits without a carry-in: s₀ = a₀ ⊕ b₀ and s₁ = a₀ ∧ b₀.
A full adder processes two input bits and a carry-in; its outputs are the sum and carry-out.
In the model considered, an HA has cost 2 and depth 1; an FA has cost 5 and depth 3.
An n-bit adder with two n-bit operands and a carry-in requires n+1 output bits.
In a ripple-carry adder, the carry propagates from the least significant to the most significant position; C(CRₙ) = 5n and D(CRₙ) = 2n+1.
A MUX selects vector a when s=1 and vector b when s=0; C(MUXₙ) = 3n+1 and D(MUXₙ) = 3.
The conditional-sum adder computes the upper half in parallel for carry-in 0 and 1; the actual lower carry then controls the MUX.
For CSA widths that are powers of two, C(CSA₁)=5, C(CSAₙ)=3C(CSAₙ/₂)+3(n/2+1)+1, and D(CSAₙ)=D(CSAₙ/₂)+3.
The CSA depth grows logarithmically; its cost grows as O(n^(log₂3)) and exceeds the ripple-carry adder's linear cost.
For n-bit two's complement, a−b ≡ a+¬b+1 modulo 2ⁿ.
A combined adder/subtractor uses sub both to XOR-invert the b bits and as the carry-in.
Signed overflow occurs exactly when the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of the sign bit.

review.notes: 45 Fragen geprüft. Fachliche Antworten, Distraktoren, Erklärungen, Quellen, Diagrammkontexte und vorhandene Verify-Skripte stimmen; keine Korrekturen oder Ersetzungen nötig.

questions.prompt: Which description fits a combinational circuit?

options.text: A directed acyclic graph with no memory
A sequence of instructions executed one after another
A memory whose contents change only when there is a carry
A graph with feedback whose output stores the next state

questions.explanation: A combinational circuit is a DAG with no memory. Its outputs depend on the current inputs.

questions.prompt: In a DIN/IEC logic-gate symbol, `≥1` denotes ___.
questions.explanation: The symbol ≥1 means that at least one input has the value 1; this is the OR function.

questions.prompt: How do you derive the canonical DNF from a truth table?

options.text: Use only the last row of the table as the circuit
Form a minterm for each row with output 0 and combine all minterms with AND
Negate all inputs and then combine them with XOR
Form a minterm for each row with output 1 and combine all minterms with OR

questions.explanation: Each row with output 1 is represented by an AND minterm; the OR of the minterms covers all rows with output 1.

source.heading: 1.3 Von Wahrheitstabelle zu Schaltung: kanonische DNF (Folien 10–12)

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct. Which equations describe a half adder?

options.text: The half adder requires a carry-in.
The sum bit is a₀ ∨ b₀.
The sum bit is a₀ ⊕ b₀.

questions.explanation: XOR produces the least significant sum bit, and AND produces the carry-out. A half adder has no carry-in.

questions.prompt: A full adder processes a carry-in in addition to the two operand bits.
questions.explanation: The carry-in comes from the previous, less significant position. Therefore, a full adder processes three input bits.

questions.prompt: A MUX selects between data vectors according to $y=(s\land a)\lor(\neg s\land b)$, for vectors $a$ and $b$. If the select bit is $s=0$, the output vector is ___.
questions.explanation: For $s=0$, $s\land a=0$ and $\neg s=1$. Therefore, the MUX outputs $b$.

questions.prompt: What does the depth D of a circuit measure?

options.text: The gates on the longest input-to-output path
All the gates in the circuit

questions.explanation: Depth measures the longest sequence of consecutive gates. Gates operating in parallel are not counted multiple times on the same path.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct. Two n-bit numbers are added with a carry-in. Which statements hold?

options.text: An output of n+1 bits is sufficient.
The carry-in cannot change the maximum value.
An output of n−1 bits is always sufficient.

questions.explanation: Two maximum-value operands plus the carry-in yield 2ⁿ⁺¹−1. This value fits in n+1 bits.

questions.prompt: Which half-adder output is the carry-out s₁?

context.content:
flowchart TB
    A["a₀"] --> XOR["XOR"]
    B["b₀"] --> XOR
    A --> AND["AND"]
    B --> AND
    XOR --> S["s₀ sum"]
    AND --> C["s₁ carry-out"]
context.caption: Signal paths in a half adder

options.text: The output of the NOT gate
The output of the XOR gate
The output of the AND gate

questions.explanation: For a half adder, s₁=a₀∧b₀. Thus, the AND gate produces the carry-out.

questions.prompt: In a ripple-carry adder, the carry propagates from the most significant to the least significant position.
questions.explanation: The carry starts at the least significant position and propagates toward the most significant position.

questions.prompt: A full adder consists of two half adders and a 2-input OR gate. The first half adder processes $a,b$ and produces a sum bit $p$ and a carry. The second processes $p$ and the carry-in, producing the final sum and a carry. The OR gate combines the two carry outputs. Each XOR, AND, and OR gate counts as one gate; depth is the number of gates on the longest input-to-output path. What are the cost $C$ and depth $D$?
questions.explanation: Each half adder contains one XOR gate and one AND gate, so the two half adders have four gates in total. Including the OR gate gives $C=4+1=5$. The longest path goes through the XOR gate of the first half adder, one gate of the second half adder, and the OR gate, giving $D=1+1+1=3$.

source.heading: 4.4 FA aus zwei HA + OR aufbauen

questions.prompt: A half adder receives a₀=1 and b₀=1. What output (s₁s₀) does it produce?
questions.explanation: 1+1=2=10₂. The more significant bit is the carry-out s₁, and the less significant bit is the sum s₀.

questions.prompt: A full adder receives a₀=1, b₀=0, and carry-in c=1. What output (s₁s₀) does it produce?
questions.explanation: The inputs give 1+0+1=2=10₂; s₁ is 1 and s₀ is 0.

questions.prompt: A 4-bit ripple-carry adder adds $0011_2$ and $0010_2$. The carry-in at the least significant bit is $0$. Calculate the sum and give it as exactly five bits, with the carry-out of the most significant bit on the left.
questions.explanation: $0011_2=3$ and $0010_2=2$, so the sum is $5=00101_2$. Bit by bit, from right to left, the sum bits are $1,0,1,0$ and the carry-out is $0$.

questions.prompt: A function y is equal to 1 exactly for the inputs (a,b)=(0,1) and (1,0). Which canonical DNF matches it?
questions.explanation: The two rows with output 1 yield the minterms ¬a∧b and a∧¬b. Their disjunction is the required DNF.

source.heading: 1.3 Von Wahrheitstabelle zu Schaltung: kanonische DNF (Folien 10–12)

questions.prompt: Calculate the cost C and depth D of a ripple-carry adder with n=4, given C=5n and D=2n+1.
questions.explanation: C=5·4=20 and D=2·4+1=9. The depth is not four times the depth of a single full adder.

questions.prompt: Calculate $6-7$ using 4-bit two's complement and give the resulting bit pattern. Use $a-b ≡ a+¬b+1$ modulo 16.
questions.explanation: The 4-bit result is (6−7) modulo 16 = 15 = 1111₂. As a signed two's-complement number, 1111 represents −1.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct. In the combined adder/subtractor, let sub=1. What must the circuit do?

options.text: Invert only the most significant bit of b
Invert each bᵢ using bᵢ ⊕ sub

questions.explanation: With sub=1, every b bit is inverted and the carry-in supplies the required +1. Together, the circuit computes a+¬b+1.

questions.prompt: In the conditional-sum adder shown, which signals determine which upper partial sum is output?

context.content:
flowchart TB
    LOW["lower bits"] --> LC["CSA with actual carry"]
    HIGH["upper bits"] --> H0["CSA with carry-in 0"]
    HIGH --> H1["CSA with carry-in 1"]
    LC -->|"carry"| MUX["MUX"]
    H0 --> MUX
    H1 --> MUX
    MUX --> OUT["upper sum and carry"]
context.caption: Parallel precomputation in the conditional-sum adder

options.text: The carry from the lower block and the two precomputed upper results
The carry-out of the most significant bit
Only the input bits of the upper half
An additional result from the lower MUX

questions.explanation: The lower block provides the actual carry. This controls the MUX, which selects between the two precomputed upper results.

source.heading: 6.1 Die zentrale Idee: parallel rechnen statt Carry abwarten

questions.prompt: Which equation describes output bit i of a 2:1 MUX with select bit s that outputs aᵢ when s=1 and bᵢ when s=0?
questions.explanation: The MUX passes aᵢ through when s=1 and bᵢ when s=0. The two AND terms are combined with OR.

questions.prompt: In a signed 4-bit two's-complement addition, $0111_2+0011_2$ causes overflow.
questions.explanation: The mathematical sum is 10, but the 4-bit two's-complement range is only −8 to 7. The result bit pattern 1010 therefore does not represent the mathematical sum.

questions.prompt: A 3-bit MUX has cost C=3n+1 and depth D=3. What are its cost and depth?
questions.explanation: For n=3, C=3·3+1=10. The depth of a MUX remains 3.

questions.prompt: The depth of a ripple-carry adder with n positions is 3n because each position contains a full adder with depth 3.
questions.explanation: On the longest carry path, the first full adder contributes three levels; each subsequent position adds two levels. Therefore, D(CRₙ)=2n+1.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct. What holds for the recursive conditional-sum adder when n>1?

options.text: Three CSA blocks of width n/2 operate in parallel.
A MUX of width n/2+1 selects the upper result together with the carry-out.
The carry must propagate through all the upper bits before they can be computed.
The upper half is computed only with carry-in 0.
The depth increases by 3 at each recursion level.

questions.explanation: A CSA processes the lower half with the actual carry and computes the upper half in parallel for carry-in 0 and 1. A MUX then selects n/2 sum bits plus the carry-out; its depth is 3.

questions.prompt: For a CSA, C(CSA₁)=5 and C(CSAₙ)=3C(CSAₙ/₂)+3(n/2+1)+1. Calculate C(CSA₂) and D(CSA₂), given D(CSA₁)=3 and D(CSAₙ)=D(CSAₙ/₂)+3.
questions.explanation: C(CSA₂)=3·5+3·2+1=22. The depth increases by 3 relative to CSA₁, so it is 6.

questions.prompt: Why do three smaller CSA circuits appear in the CSA recurrence step?

options.text: Each half is computed three times in sequence.
All three compute the same upper half with carry-in 0.
One computes the lower half with the actual carry; two compute the upper half for carry-in 0 and 1.
One circuit computes the sum, one the carry, and one the overflow.

questions.explanation: The lower CSA provides the actual carry. The two upper CSA blocks provide results for both possible carry-in values.

questions.prompt: The naive canonical DNF can become expensive for n input bits because the truth table has ___ rows.
questions.explanation: n binary inputs have 2ⁿ possible assignments. Therefore, the direct construction can grow quickly as n increases.

source.heading: 1.3 Von Wahrheitstabelle zu Schaltung: kanonische DNF (Folien 10–12)

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct. Which statements apply to signed overflow in two's-complement addition?

options.text: Equal carries at these two positions mean there is no overflow.
Overflow occurs when the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of the sign bit.
An ordinary unsigned carry and signed overflow are the same thing.
A carry-out alone reliably detects signed overflow.

questions.explanation: The overflow test is the XOR of the two carries at the sign bit. A carry-out alone is not sufficient because signed overflow is a different property.

questions.prompt: A 4-bit MUX selects vector a when s=1 and vector b when s=0. Let a=1010, b=0110, and s=0. What is the output?
questions.explanation: When s=0, the MUX selects vector b. Therefore, the output is 0110.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, what goes from the lower block to the MUX, and what is its purpose?

context.content:
flowchart LR
    LOW["lower CSA"] -->|"carry"| MUX["MUX"]
    H0["upper CSA: carry-in 0"] --> MUX
    H1["upper CSA: carry-in 1"] --> MUX
    MUX --> OUT["upper result"]
context.caption: The lower carry controls the selection of the upper result

options.text: The least significant sum bit; it is reused as the carry-in.
The upper carry-out; it selects the lower block.
An overflow flag; it inverts both upper results.
The actual carry; it controls the selection of the upper result.

questions.explanation: The carry from the lower half determines whether the upper result for carry-in 0 or carry-in 1 is selected.

source.heading: 6.1 Die zentrale Idee: parallel rechnen statt Carry abwarten

questions.prompt: Two gates operate in parallel on separate input-to-output paths. What are their combined cost and depth?
questions.explanation: Both gates count toward the cost, so C=2. Because they operate in parallel, the longest path contains only one gate level.

questions.prompt: In a combined adder/subtractor, sub=1 must both XOR each b bit and set the carry-in to 1.
questions.explanation: The XOR operations invert b; the carry-in adds 1. Without the carry-in, the second step of two's complement would be missing.

questions.prompt: Add $0111_2+0011_2$ as signed 4-bit two's-complement numbers. What result bit pattern is produced, and does overflow occur?
questions.explanation: The bitwise addition gives 1010. Both operands are positive, but the result bit pattern is negative; also, the carry into and out of the sign bit differ, so overflow occurs.

questions.prompt: Can a half adder be built using only NAND gates?

options.text: Yes, but only if an additional carry-in is available.
No, because NAND cannot implement negation.
No, because a half adder must use an OR gate.
Yes, because NAND alone is functionally complete.

questions.explanation: NAND is functionally complete and can therefore represent any Boolean function, including the half adder's sum and carry functions.

questions.prompt: Add the 4-bit two's-complement numbers $0111_2$ and $0001_2$. Give the 4-bit result and state whether signed overflow occurs.
questions.explanation: The sum 8 is outside the 4-bit two's-complement range [−8,7]. The pattern is 1000; the carry into and out of the sign bit differ.

questions.prompt: A 4-bit adder/subtractor is to compute $0110_2-0010_2$. Use $a-b\equiv a+\neg b+1\pmod{16}$: invert all bits of $b$, add $1$, and keep the four least significant result bits. What 4-bit result is produced?
questions.explanation: $\neg 0010_2=1101_2$. Then $0110_2+1101_2+1=10100_2$. The four least significant bits are $0100_2$.

questions.prompt: Compare the model values for a ripple-carry adder and a conditional-sum adder when n=8. For CR, C=5n and D=2n+1. For CSA, C(CSA₁)=5, C(CSAₙ)=3C(CSAₙ/₂)+3(n/2+1)+1, and D(CSA₁)=3 and D(CSAₙ)=D(CSAₙ/₂)+3.
questions.explanation: For CR₈, C=40 and D=17. The CSA recurrence gives C=244 and D=12: more gates, but less depth.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct. Which statements correctly describe the architectural trade-off?

options.text: The ripple-carry adder computes the upper half in advance for both carry cases.
The conditional-sum adder uses more hardware to reduce carry wait time.
The ripple-carry adder has linear cost and linear depth.
The conditional-sum adder has logarithmic depth and cost O(n^(log₂3)).

questions.explanation: The ripple-carry adder is simple, with both cost and depth growing linearly. The CSA computes additional carry cases in parallel: its depth is logarithmic, while its cost grows faster than linearly.

source.heading: 9. Architekturvergleich – was ist die eigentliche Idee?

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct. A conditional-sum adder should also be able to subtract. What must hold for sub=1?

options.text: All b bits are XORed with sub.
A MUX can select between the precomputed carry cases.
The upper CSA half must be computed only with carry-in 0.

questions.explanation: sub=1 inverts b and sets the carry-in to 1, producing a+¬b+1. The CSA structure can provide the possible carry cases in parallel and select between them with a MUX.

questions.prompt: A 4-bit adder receives a=0110, b=0011, and carry-in 1. What five output bits are produced?
questions.explanation: 6+3+1=10. In five bits, the result is 01010₂; the carry-in must be included in the addition.

questions.prompt: In the adder/subtractor circuit shown, which two connections must the control bit sub control?

context.content:
flowchart LR
    B["b bits"] --> XOR["XOR gates"]
    SUB["sub"] --> XOR
    SUB -->|"carry-in"| ADD["adder"]
    A["a bits"] --> ADD
    XOR -->|"b-prime"| ADD
    ADD --> OUT["result"]
context.caption: Control paths in the combined adder/subtractor

options.text: Only the adder output and the overflow flag
The XOR gates for the b bits and the adder's carry-in
Only the XOR gates for the b bits

questions.explanation: sub controls both the conditional inversion of each b bit and the carry-in. Thus, sub=1 gives the computation a+¬b+1.

questions.prompt: Which condition tests for overflow in a signed two's-complement addition?

options.text: The carry-out from the sign bit is 1.
The carry into the sign bit XOR the carry out of the sign bit is 1.
The two carry values at the sign bit are equal.
The least significant sum bit is 1.

questions.explanation: Overflow occurs when the two carries at the sign bit differ. Their XOR is then 1.

questions.prompt: A Boolean function y is 1 for (a,b)=(0,1) and (1,1), and 0 otherwise. Which of the listed functions agrees for all inputs?
questions.explanation: In both rows with output 1, b=1; in the remaining rows, b=0. Thus, y=b describes the table and is the simplified form of the canonical DNF.

source.heading: 1.3 Von Wahrheitstabelle zu Schaltung: kanonische DNF (Folien 10–12)

questions.prompt: Two 3-bit operands are both at their maximum value, and the adder receives carry-in 1. How many bits are needed, and what result is produced?
questions.explanation: 111₂+111₂+1₂=15=1111₂. Two 3-bit operands plus a carry-in require at most four output bits.

levels.title: In Practice: Logic in Everyday Life

questions.prompt: At any moment, a heating controller receives only two signals: `kalt` and `fenster_zu`. It turns the heating on exactly when both signals are 1. The component stores no previous values. Which type of circuit fits?

options.text: A circuit with memory that retains previous measurements.
A half adder that adds two bits without a carry-in.
A combinational circuit: the output depends only on the current inputs.
A ripple-carry adder that propagates a carry across several positions.

questions.explanation: The described block has no memory: given the same current input signals, it produces the same output. This is the definition of a combinational circuit.

questions.prompt: A wearable device should use the same arithmetic unit to add or subtract. `sub=0` means addition, and `sub=1` means subtraction. When `sub=1`, which hardware connections are needed to compute $a-b$?

options.text: XOR each bit of $b$ with `sub`: $b'_i=b_i\oplus sub$.
Set only the carry-in to 1 and leave $b$ unchanged.
Invert the bits of $a$ and set the carry-in to 0.

questions.explanation: When `sub=1`, $b$ is inverted and a carry-in of 1 is added. The device therefore computes $a+\neg b+1$, which gives $a-b$ modulo the bit width.

questions.prompt: A 4-bit adder receives two 4-bit operands. Each possible ordered pair of operands counts as one input case. How many input cases are there in total?
questions.explanation: Each operand has $2^4=16$ possible bit patterns. For two operands, there are $16\cdot16=256$ ordered pairs.

questions.prompt: A game stores the score as a signed 4-bit number. The representable range is $[-8,7]$. After $+7+3$, the counter displays the bit pattern `1010`. What should the overflow indicator report?

options.text: Overflow occurs only if unsigned addition also produces a carry-out.
No overflow: the sum fits in four bits when interpreted as unsigned.
No overflow: `1010` is a valid 4-bit pattern.
Signed overflow: the mathematical sum 10 is outside $[-8,7]$.

questions.explanation: $7+3=10$ is greater than the largest representable 4-bit two's-complement value, 7. The pattern `1010` represents a valid number, but it represents $-6$ rather than 10: signed overflow has occurred.

questions.prompt: A display pipeline computes two possible pixel values: A=`0110` and B=`1101`. A MUX is a switch: when $s=1$, it outputs A; when $s=0$, it outputs B. What is the output when $s=1$?
questions.explanation: When $s=1$, the MUX selects vector A. In a pipeline, for example, this selection can switch between two already computed pixel values.

questions.prompt: In the simplified gate model, a ripple-carry adder with $n$ bits has depth $D=2n+1$. What is the depth of a 12-bit adder?
questions.explanation: Substitute $n=12$: $D=2\cdot12+1=25$. Depth counts the gates along the longest input-to-output path.

questions.prompt: You are designing the logic for a badge reader and may use only NAND gates in your gate model. Which practical fact about NAND helps you?

options.text: NAND can output 1 only when both inputs are 1.
NAND gates automatically store previous input values.
Any Boolean function can be built from NAND gates alone.
NAND can represent only functions with exactly two inputs.

questions.explanation: NAND is functionally complete: by connecting NAND gates appropriately, you can implement any Boolean function. This is useful when a design is restricted to a single gate type.

questions.prompt: For a conditional-sum adder with power-of-two widths $n$: $C(CSA_1)=5$, and for $n>1$, $C(CSA_n)=3C(CSA_{n/2})+3(n/2+1)+1$. Recursively calculate the number of gates for $CSA_8$. Count all gates according to this cost formula.

In a door-control system, $a$ and $b$ are input bits. The enable signal $y$ is 1 exactly for $(a,b)=(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$, and is 0 otherwise. Which formula is the canonical DNF, with a separate minterm for each row with output 1?
questions.explanation: The canonical DNF forms one minterm for each of the two rows with $y=1$ and combines them with OR. Here, the formula can then be simplified to $b$.

source.heading: 1.3 Von Wahrheitstabelle zu Schaltung: kanonische DNF (Folien 10–12)

questions.prompt: You are planning a 32-bit arithmetic core for a device where short addition time is important and more chip area is available. A ripple-carry adder saves gates, but its carry propagates one position at a time. A conditional-sum adder computes upper partial results in parallel for carry-in 0 and 1, then selects between them with a MUX. Which concept better fits the timing goal?

options.text: Conditional-sum adder: more hardware, but logarithmically growing depth.
Canonical DNF: it selects between both adder results using a MUX.
Half adder: it processes the carry-in of the upper half.
Ripple-carry adder: its carry path grows logarithmically.

questions.explanation: The conditional-sum adder computes both possible carry cases in parallel, then uses a MUX to select between them. It requires more gates but reduces depth compared with the ripple adder's linear carry chain.
